title: More time doesn't mean better work

source.citation: Ariely, D., & Wertenbroch, K. (2002). Procrastination, deadlines, and performance: Self-control by precommitment. Psychological Science, 13(3), 219-224.
source.finding: In a proofreading experiment, people given evenly spaced deadlines found the most errors and were least late; people with one final deadline did worst; people who set their own deadlines came in between.
source.caveat: This is one well-known study with small groups of adults, not a body of repeated findings. One of its authors, Dan Ariely, has since had other papers retracted over data problems; I am not aware of concerns raised about this paper, but check before publishing.

scenes.narration: Having more time doesn't get you better work.
A deadline that's weeks away sounds great. Loads of time. No pressure.
In 2002, researchers gave people three pieces of work. Some had one deadline at the end. Others had three, spaced out.
The spaced-out group did the best work. The one-big-deadline group did the worst.
People who set their own deadlines landed in between. It helped, but not as much.
Today, split one piece of coursework into three parts. Give each a date. Tell someone who'll ask.
